result.summary: Earth, angry over the Titans, bears the giants, and the gods defeat them with Hercules' help since an oracle says a mortal is needed. Earth then bears Typhon, who drives the gods to flee to Egypt, and Zeus after a hard struggle finally buries him under Mount Etna.

scenes.title: Birth of the giants
scenes.summary: Earth bears the giants, who attack heaven. Because of an oracle, Zeus summons Hercules, who kills Alcyoneus by dragging him out of his native land.
scenes.stakes: The gods risk defeat unless a mortal helps them, while Earth tries to protect the giants.

scenes.title: Battle of gods and giants
scenes.summary: Porphyrion attacks Hera and is killed. The gods each slay other giants, and Hercules finishes them with arrows.
scenes.stakes: Hera is threatened with violation, and the gods' victory depends on destroying every giant.

scenes.title: Typhon attacks heaven
scenes.summary: Earth bears the monstrous Typhon in Cilicia. He assaults heaven and the gods flee to Egypt in animal forms.
scenes.stakes: The gods' rule over heaven is threatened.

scenes.title: Zeus defeated and maimed
scenes.summary: Zeus fights Typhon at Mount Casius, loses his sinews and is hidden in the Corycian cave. Hermes and Aegipan steal the sinews back.
scenes.stakes: Zeus is crippled and captive, and could lose his power.

scenes.title: Typhon pursued and buried
scenes.summary: Restored Zeus chases Typhon through Nysa and Thrace, where he is wounded at Haemus, then buries him under Etna.
scenes.stakes: Typhon fights for survival; Zeus must secure his rule.

notable_quotes.reason: The oracle that gods alone cannot kill the giants, requiring a mortal's help.

analysis.text: Order against chaos: Earth's monstrous children challenge the Olympians, and victory needs cunning and a mortal ally as well as force.

Typhon's battle sites in Cilicia, Syria, Thrace and Sicily link the myth to volcanic and eastern Mediterranean landscapes, and the flight to Egypt echoes Greek links between animal-headed Egyptian gods and their own.

legacy.text: Gigantomachy was a favorite subject of Greek art, as on the Pergamon Altar, and Typhon's burial under Etna became the traditional explanation of volcanic eruptions.

fun_facts.text: The name Typhon is the root of the word 'typhoon' in some etymological accounts.

language_notes.text: The Titans were Earth's earlier children, imprisoned in Tartarus by Zeus; Earth's anger at this punishment motivates the giants' birth.
Phlegrae ("burning") and Pallene are places in northern Greece (Chalcidice) traditionally named as the battlefield of the gods and giants.
Erythia is the western island where Hercules took the cattle of Geryones; the Sun's cows are a separate herd, so this is a different tradition.
"Made an end of" means destroyed or killed.
"Simple" means a medicinal herb or plant; here a magical plant that would make the giants immune to death even by a mortal.
A thyrsus is a staff tipped with a pine cone and wreathed in ivy, carried by Dionysus and his followers.
The helmet of Hades made its wearer invisible, so Hermes could fight unseen.
'Brazer' is likely a misprint for 'brazen', meaning made of bronze.
Adamantine means made of adamant, a legendary unbreakable metal.
Ephemeral fruits are short-lived, mortal fruits. Typhon is tricked into thinking they will strengthen him; in fact they weaken him.
The name Haemus is explained by Greek haima, 'blood'; this is an ancient folk etymology.

context_notes.text: Sky (Uranus) is Earth's husband and the father of the Titans; the giants are a second brood born from his blood and Earth.
Hercules was a mortal son of Zeus, which is why the gods needed him; Athena often guides heroes with advice.
Zeus's trick makes Porphyrion's assault on Hera lead to his own destruction, since it gives the gods a pretext to kill him.
Athena, goddess of war and wisdom, is often shown wearing the aegis, a protective skin or cloak.
Tartarus is the deepest region of the underworld; here Earth takes him as her mate to produce Typhon.
Egyptian gods had animal forms, and Greek writers explained this by saying the Olympians once hid there as animals.
Delphyne is a serpent guardian, linked to Delphi in some versions of the myth.

literary_notes.text: Vivid physical detail of long hair, beards and dragon-scale feet makes the giants monstrous and sets them apart from the Olympian gods.
Zeus darkens the heavenly lights to keep the herb hidden, so the sky itself is used as a tool against Earth's plan.
The earlier remark that Alcyoneus is immortal only in his native land prepares for his defeat by being dragged beyond its border.
Typhon towering over mountains and brushing the stars conveys his monstrous scale.
Hurled burning rocks, hissing, shouting and spouted fire create a vivid, overwhelming picture of assault on heaven.
Typhon eats the fruit to gain strength but is undone by it, reversing his intention.
